title: He Who Was Rich Became Poor
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Context of Human Brokenness
subpoints: Christ entered a world marred by sin and rebellion
Understanding human limitation highlights the necessity of Christ's mission
The incarnation is a response to humanity's need for salvation

outline.title: The Theological Keystone of 2 Corinthians 8-9
subpoints: Verse 9 serves as the foundation for the appeal to give
Christ's voluntary self-impoverishment is the pattern for Christian generosity
Every command in the chapter is an outworking of this grace

outline.title: The Riches of Christ Prior to Incarnation
subpoints: Rich in pre-existence: The Word was with God and was God
Rich in possessions: Christ owns all creation
Rich in power: The agent of all creation
Rich in honor: Praised by angels and sharing the Father's glory
Rich in love: Perfect harmony within the Trinity

outline.title: The Mystery of the Incarnation
subpoints: The infinite step downward from divine glory to human nature
The surprise of the angels at the Son taking on a human nature
The paradox of the immutable God adding a human nature without change to the divine

summary:
The sermon explores the theological depth of 2 Corinthians 8:9, identifying it as the keystone of Paul's appeal for generosity in the Corinthian church. The message begins by establishing the context of human brokenness, emphasizing that Christ entered a world corrupted by sin, not a neutral or perfect one. This understanding of humanity's rebellion and need for salvation highlights the magnitude of Christ's mission to save His people from their sins.

The central focus is on the paradox of Christ's nature: He who was rich became poor for the sake of believers. The sermon details the specific dimensions of Christ's pre-incarnate riches, including His eternal pre-existence, His ownership of all creation, His creative power, His divine honor shared with the Father, and the perfect love within the Trinity. These attributes underscore the voluntary nature of His self-impoverishment.

Finally, the sermon addresses the mystery of the incarnation, describing it as the greatest surprise in Christian theology. It highlights the infinite step downward taken by the Son of God, who laid aside His crown and glory to take on human nature. This act of grace is presented not merely as a historical event but as the foundational pattern for Christian living, particularly in the context of sacrificial giving and the transformation of the believer's heart.
